name: Georgian
variety: Standard Georgian, based on the Kartlian dialect and spoken in Tbilisi
sources: Shosted, Ryan K. & Chikovani, Vakhtang (2006). Standard Georgian. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 36(2): 255-264.

Vicenik, Chad (2010). An acoustic study of Georgian stop consonants. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 40(1): 59-92. The figures used here are from the preprint in UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 107.
Wysocki, Tamra (2004). Acoustic analysis of Georgian stop consonants and stop clusters. PhD dissertation, University of Washington. Cited from Vicenik (2010).
Robins, R. H. & Waterson, Natalie (1952). Notes on the phonetics of the Georgian word. Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 14.
Butskhrikidze, Marika (2002). The Consonant Phonotactics of Georgian. Utrecht: LOT.
Chitoran, Ioana (1998). Georgian harmonic clusters: phonetic cues to phonological representation. Phonology 15: 121-141.
Aronson, Howard I. (1997). Georgian phonology. In Alan S. Kaye (ed.), Phonologies of Asia and Africa, vol. 2, 929-939. Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns.

Vicenik, Chad & Jun, Sun-Ah (2014). An autosegmental-metrical analysis of Georgian intonation. In Sun-Ah Jun (ed.), Prosodic Typology II: The Phonology of Intonation and Phrasing. Oxford University Press.
Borise, Lena & Zientarski, Xavier (2018). Word stress and phrase accent in Georgian. Proceedings of Tonal Aspects of Languages (TAL) 2018.
Borise, Lena (2023). Disentangling word stress and phrasal prosody: a view from Georgian. Phonological Data and Analysis 5(1): 1-37.
Beguš, Gašper (2021). Segmental phonetics and phonology in Caucasian languages. In Maria Polinsky (ed.), The Oxford Handbook of Languages of the Caucasus. Oxford University Press.
contrasts: three-way laryngeal contrast in stops and affricates: voiced, voiceless aspirated, ejective
one uvular, the ejective /qʼ/, with no plain or voiced partner
five vowels, no length, no nasalisation, no diphthongs
no contrastive stress and no gemination within morphemes
allophony: the voiced stops are weakly voiced: on average 75% of the closure is voiced between vowels, and word-initially, word-finally and in clusters they are often voiceless unaspirated (Robins & Waterson 1952; Vicenik 2010)
the three series differ in voicing lag: aspirated longest, ejective intermediate, voiced shortest. Closure duration does not separate them (about 71 ms at the start of a phrase, 56 ms word-medially)

ejectives at the start of a phrase have a silent gap between the burst and the vowel, caused by the late release of the glottis; word-medially the oral and glottal releases are nearly simultaneous and the lag is close to that of the voiced stops
the vowel after an ejective begins with creaky voice and flat or rising F0; after aspirated and voiced stops F0 falls, and after aspirated stops the onset is breathier (Vicenik 2010)
about 17% of the closure of aspirated stops and 27% of the closure of ejectives is voiced when a vowel precedes
/qʼ/ varies freely between an ejective stop [qʼ], an affricated stop, an ejective fricative [χʼ] and a glottal stop; the neighbouring vowels are laryngealised
/x ɣ/ are velar for some speakers and uvular for others
/r/ is a tap with a closure of about 20 ms, sometimes a trill of two contacts
/v/ is [v] in most positions, [f] or [ɸ] before a voiceless consonant, a rounded offglide [ʷ] after a voiceless obstruent, and may be dropped before /u/
/i u/ are tense and /ɛ ɔ/ lax; /ɑ/ has a low F2 but is unrounded
in connected speech clusters are reduced: nasals are vocalised or dropped and /r/ is dropped
a stop may emerge between a nasal and a fricative: /mzɛ/ 'sun' is [mbzɛ]
phonotactics: onsets of up to six consonants in lexical words and eight with prefixes (/mtsʼvrtʰnɛli/ 'trainer', /ɡvpʰrtsʰkʰvni/ 'you peel us')
harmonic clusters: a labial or coronal obstruent followed by a velar or uvular one of the same laryngeal type (dɡ, tʰkʰ, tʼkʼ, tsʼqʼ) behave as single units
sonorants inside long clusters may be syllabic
adjacent vowels belong to different syllables
the nominative ending makes most nouns end in /i/ or another vowel

stress.rule: Stress falls on the first syllable of every word; the pitch prominence heard on the antepenult or penult of longer words belongs to the phrase, not to the word (Borise 2023).
stress.cues: duration only: the first syllable is longer than all later ones (about 218 ms against 181 ms for the second syllable); intensity falls steadily through the word; F0 is used by phrasal tones and disappears in deaccented words

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none; every vowel keeps its quality
rhythm.notes: No rhythm-metric classification is cited. Syllables vary greatly in complexity because of the consonant clusters, while vowels are not reduced.

length.notes: No length contrast. Identical consonants meet only across morpheme boundaries.

voice_onset_time_ms.source: Vicenik 2010, voicing lag at the start of an accentual phrase, five female speakers, words in carrier phrases and stories
voice_onset_time_ms.notes: The measure is voicing lag, which is never negative; the voiced stops have most of their closure voiced when a vowel precedes. Utterance-initial lags are longer for the ejectives (26, 49 and 59 ms for labial, alveolar and velar) and word-medial lags are shorter for all series (aspirated 40-51, ejective 16-30, voiced 2-16). Wysocki (2004) found longer lags in word lists: about 90 ms aspirated, 50 ms ejective, 20 ms voiced.

intonation.declarative: each word forms an accentual phrase with a low accent on its first syllable and a rise to a high boundary on its last syllable; the peaks step down from phrase to phrase, and the last phrase falls to a low boundary
intonation.yes_no_question: word order of a statement; the verb carries a phrase accent, low on its penultimate syllable (often after a high antepenult), followed by a sharp rise on the final syllable
intonation.wh_question: the question word stands before the verb and carries the main peak; the verb has the low phrase accent on its penult; the sentence ends low or with a rise-fall
intonation.continuation: high boundary at the end of every non-final accentual phrase
intonation.accent_shape: L* on the initial syllable, with the steepest rise and the peak inside the final syllable of the word
intonation.notes: After Vicenik & Jun (2014) and Borise (2023). Two or three related words may form an intermediate phrase, in which non-final words have a high accent and low boundary instead. Words after a narrow focus may lose their tones.

phonation: ejective stops and affricates, with creaky voice at the start of the following vowel
breathier vowel onset after aspirated stops
creaky voice is frequent in connected speech

problems: There are no ejectives. პ ტ კ are the plain unaspirated stops p-, t-, k- of the consonants table, წ is an unaspirated [ts] and ყ is the plain uvular stop q; the ejective recordings in phsource/ustop are not used.
ჭ /tʃʼ/ is the phoneme c (consonants/c2, a palatalised affricate with the IPA name c), so it differs from ჩ in place as well as in release.
/qʼ/ has none of its fricative or glottal variants, and ღ and ხ are always velar.
ვ is always [v]: no [f] or [ɸ] before voiceless consonants and no rounding after obstruents.

Stress is strong: primary on the first syllable with secondary stresses on alternate later syllables (sˈakʰartʰvˌelo, mˈastsavlˌebeli) and the Tamil stress lengths and amplitudes. The literature describes weak initial stress cued by duration alone.

A schwa is inserted inside the longest clusters, after r (მწვრთნელი gives [mtsvrətʰnˈeli]) and after the first consonant of გვფრცქვნი, where the inserted vowel even takes a primary stress ([ɡˈəvpʰrətsʰkʰvnˈi]).
რ is the trill R; the literature describes a tap.
The default intonation tunes are used: no rise at the end of each word and no low penult in questions.
good: the three stop series are kept apart as voiced, aspirated (p#, t#, k#, ts#) and unaspirated
five vowels with open-mid e and o
long consonant clusters are read as words, not spelled out
one letter, one phoneme, as in the orthography

notes: For the ejectives a synthesiser needs a burst, a short silent interval (longer at the start of a phrase) and a creaky vowel onset; aspiration noise must be absent. No formant figures are given: Shosted & Chikovani (2006) publish a vowel chart for one male speaker but no table.
